genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the goldsmith avoids setting stones at the end of the day because her hands tremble
her mother practised the same craft in front of her during her childhood
watching her mother settled her choice of trade
the lack of fine tools in the family workshop forced her to improvise
she smoothed her pieces with a hide stretched over a wooden block
that early constraint gave her great patience
her work is known for holding fast and staying free of scratches
her refusal of short deadlines lengthens the queue of her customers
she maintains that haste always leaves a mark in the material
text: By evening her hands shake, just a little, and that is why she settled long ago on a rule she has never broken: no stone goes into its setting once the light has gone. As a child she watched her mother tilt a blade against warm metal, and the sight settled the question of what she would do with her life. The family workshop held no tool fine enough for the job, so she learnt to smooth her pieces on a hide stretched over a block of wood, and the slowness of it left her with a patience out of the ordinary. That is what lies behind the name she carries now: her settings hold, and her surfaces come away unscratched. Because she turns down anything hurried, the queue of people waiting on her grows longer every season. Rush the material, she says, and it keeps the mark of it.

units: the product is criticised because it sets too early
a dry mark appears across wide surfaces and can no longer be removed
the thinner lifts too quickly in heated rooms
the maker advises adding an additive that slows the drying
this additive does not weaken the final coat
he also advises laying it on in thin overlapping bands
tests on hardwood confirm the improvement
the scraping tool must be honed before each application
the assessment is mixed and depends on the willingness to change one's practice
text: The complaint that follows this varnish everywhere is that it grabs too soon. Brushed across a wide panel, it begins to set before the brush has finished its run, and the dry edge left behind can never be worked out again. Examination points to the thinner, which lifts far too fast in a heated room. The maker offers an answer in two parts. A retarder, poured in small amount, stretches the working time without weakening the cured coat. The second part is about the hand: lay the varnish on in narrow bands that overlap, never in broad sweeps. Trials on hardwood panels bear the gain out, provided the scraper is honed before each coat. The judgement therefore stays mixed. It is a demanding product, dependable for anyone willing to rework their habits, disappointing for anyone who wants a result straight away.

units: the writer is writing from a workshop recommended by his correspondent
the rods are sorted before the weaving in this place
the objects made keep their shape once dry
in the earlier workshop the pace was faster
the pieces from the earlier workshop lost their shape quickly
the former teacher merely showed a movement to copy
the present teacher breaks down each movement and allows mistakes
the writer advances more slowly but remembers more
the difficult stages are carried out in silence in this new workshop
text: I am writing from the basket workshop you recommended to me, and I should like to set out what separates it from the last. Here the rods are sorted before any weaving begins, and the difference tells: the baskets keep their curve once they have dried. Where I was before, the pace was quicker, but the pieces lost their shape within days. The teaching differs as well. My former master would show a movement and wait for me to copy it, whereas the one here breaks every movement down and lets me get it wrong without stepping in. I come on more slowly, and I remember far more. The room itself is unlike the other, too: the delicate stages are done in silence, where the old workshop hummed with talk. I thank you for pointing me towards this place, and I send you my respectful regards.

units: three qualities are named as conditions for entering this trade
the folding tool must be held without stiffening the wrist
a tightened wrist sends the fold off course
the shades of the covering materials must agree whatever the light in the room
the sequence of operations for the rounded spine cannot be altered
the workshops say the training has no set length
a beginner's progress is described as uneven
those who practise the trade name the freedom of the hand among its rewards
mending a damaged object brings a satisfaction the practitioners mention
text: What is asked of anyone who wants a place in a bookbinding workshop? Three aptitudes come up again and again in the masters' answers. The first belongs to the hand: the folder is held without stiffening the wrist, or the fold runs off at an angle. The second belongs to the eye, since leather and cloth must agree with one another under a dim light as surely as under a bright one. The third is a matter of remembering movements, because a rounded spine comes out of a sequence whose order will bear no swapping. And the training, how long does it run? The workshops answer that it has no set end, and that a careful beginner comes on in uneven steps. What is there to gain from so exacting a path? Those who practise it name the freedom of the hand, the variety of the work, and the pleasure of seeing a ruined volume put back into use.

units: the beginner turned up before the appointed hour
he asked for permission to handle the cutting tools
the craftsman refused and gave him a cleaning task
the request was made again seven days later
the craftsman then supplied a metal plate and asked for a straight line
the line that came out ran off course
the craftsman corrected the position of the tool and of the finger without any remark
the next day's line was distinctly better
the craftsman played the success down by mentioning how many lines would be needed
he quietly admitted having done worse at the same age
text: The apprentice turned up ahead of time and asked the engraver outright whether he was allowed to touch the burins. Not yet, said the master, who handed him a broom instead and laughed about it. A week on, the lad came back and asked the same thing again. This time the engraver put a copper plate down on the bench and told him to try cutting one straight line, nothing more. The line wandered off to one side. The master made no criticism of it; he only showed him how to angle the tool and where the thumb belongs. The next day the apprentice cut a line that was almost clean, and he made rather a lot of it. One line is not a trade, the engraver told him, and it would take thousands of them before he had any right to talk like that. Then he added, more quietly, that his own had been less straight at the same age.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: the widening of the trade routes brought more orders than the workshops could handle
the craftsmen changed the way they bent the boards
round hearths replaced heating each piece on its own
several boards were softened at the same time
the vessels that came out had identical measurements
the merchants could work out the size of their loads in advance
disagreements over the quantities carried grew fewer
the rise in demand called for more young people in training
the trade bodies made entry to the craft harder
the fear of seeing the craft weakened led to a setting of the movements into rules
text: As the trading routes widened, the cooperages found themselves with more orders than they could ever fill. The pressure pushed the craftsmen to rethink the way they bent their staves: instead of heating each piece on its own, they built round hearths where a dozen boards softened together. The change carried a consequence nobody had looked for. Since the casks now came out to the same measurements, merchants could work their loads out in advance, and quarrels about the quantities delivered fell away. Standard sizes fed the demand, and the demand called for more apprentices. The trade bodies then tightened their rules of entry, afraid of watching the craft thin out. Out of that fear grew the long setting of the movements into rules that the workshops kept up long afterwards.

units: an uneven surface takes up the colour unevenly
dark patches appear instead of a smooth gradation
wood cut across its fibres drinks more of the product
the correction rests on a graded run of abrasives
one starts with a harsh abrasive that removes the ridges left by the tool
no intermediate grade may be skipped
each abrasive removes only the marks of the one before it
the final smoothing follows the direction of the fibres
wetting the wood before the last pass raises the fibres so that they can be laid down for good
text: A rough surface drinks the stain unevenly, and the craftsman who overlooks so small a thing finds dark patches spreading where he had hoped for a soft gradation. The fault lies in the grain itself: cut across, it opens and swallows three or four drops where flat grain will take only one. The remedy is a patient climb. Begin with a biting abrasive, which levels off the ridges the blade has left behind. Move on to a medium grit, then to a fine one, and never skip a stage, since each paper takes out nothing but the scratches of the one before it. Polish last of all along the run of the grain, and wet the wood before the final pass, so that the fibres it raises may be laid down for good. The surface then comes smooth under the palm, and the stain settles across it in one even tone.

units: two cutting edges were shown to a doubting beginner
the first edge was ground to a close angle
it took long shavings in a soft wood
it buckled on meeting a hard patch in the wood
the second edge had a more open angle
it damaged the soft fibre and left an uneven bottom
it went through the hard patches without harm
the conclusion drawn is that a tool can be judged only against its use
the close angle is kept for finishing passes
the open angle suits the quick removal of material
text: Two blades laid side by side on the bench served as the lesson for a trainee who doubted that angles mattered. The first, a plane iron ground to a close angle, bit into soft wood in unbroken shavings, yet it crumpled the moment it entered a knotty log. The second, ground blunter, tore the soft fibre and left a ragged bottom, and still it crossed the knot without flinching. The workshop drew its conclusion: a tool is worth nothing apart from the job it is meant for. So the keen edge is kept for finishing, where what comes away is counted in the thinnest of slivers, and the stout edge for roughing out, when shifting bulk matters more than the surface left behind. The trainee held on to the rule and put it in his own words: you choose an angle against the material, not against the man beside you.

units: four supplies must be gathered on the working surface
the suppleness of the rods is checked by bending them
rods that are too stiff must soak for about sixty minutes
the assembly starts with eight rods crossed in the shape of a star
the centre is held down with the finger during the weaving
each pass must be drawn tight against the one before without any sideways pull
the upright rods are then raised to form the sides
evenness is checked by holding the object at eye level
the top edge is folded inwards and then held with a stitched seam
the drying is done flat and away from any source of heat
text: Before you begin, set out on the bench the following: a bundle of softened fibres, a curved needle, waxed thread and a pair of straight-bladed scissors. Check that the rods will bend without cracking; should they resist, soak them and leave them there for an hour. Turn next to the setting-up. Cross eight rods in a star, hold the centre down under your thumb, then weave, drawing each pass tight against the one before it and never pulling to one side. Raising the walls comes next. Bring the uprights up one by one and carry the weave round in a spiral, checking the evenness at eye level. Finish the piece. Cut the ends on the slant, turn the top edge inwards over the uprights, and stitch right round with waxed thread. Leave the work to dry flat, well away from any source of heat.

units: a demonstration open to the public is taking place in a forge in an old district
the craftswoman lit her fire and told the public what she would be doing
the metal brought to a high heat was curved with the hammer
those watching saw the colours of the piece change
the piece was cooled in a trough
a file served to even out the surface
the craftswoman pointed out that strength does not rule out a fine finish
children were invited to hold the gripping tool
an opening one evening a week was announced
the neighbours will be able to follow the making of a grille
text: Onlookers are pressing round the forge in the old quarter of the town, where a public demonstration has just opened. Early in the afternoon the smith lit her hearth and told the crowd gathered there what she meant to make. An hour later the bar came out of the coals glowing and took its curve under measured blows of the hammer. Those watching saw the piece pass from white to brown, then darken in the quenching trough. The smith next took up a file and brought the surface smooth, remarking that strength is no excuse for rough work. Towards the close of the afternoon she invited the youngest of them to hold the tongs while she struck. The session ended on an announcement: the workshop will open one evening a week, so that the neighbourhood may follow the making of a balcony grille.
